doc.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

chapter: The music business and jazz education
title: Finding your own sound: Coltrane's openness to influences
summary: Coltrane loved everybody, including Junior Walker; students with fake books and transcriptions risk losing identity, per Michael Brecker.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Because you know what happens is a person is not really searching for their sound. I mean as much as John Coltrane loved Dexter Gordon and Sonny Rollins and he would tell you he loved everybody because he was influenced by all these people. I mean I’ll never forget somebody was interviewing him and he was saying well who’s your influences and he said, “Well I love Dexter and I love Sonny Rollins,” and he said, “really everybody.” I mean there was nobody that did not influence him. And I remember my father telling a very poignant story, he said he and John were in Detroit one night and they went around the corner to go hear Junior Walker play. And it was like he said John Coltrane said, “Man how does Junior Walker play those high A’s on his back like that.” And he said, “I’d give my left arm to play a high — I mean it is just so effortless. He said how does he do that? Because he was checking out Junior Walker. He said you would never think that. But that’s the kind of musician he was. He wasn’t this person who — as great as he was he realized his greatness came from everybody, his influences. So he never wanted to lose that. And I think now what happens is like these kids are so quick and they grasp concepts and they go to school now and like you say you have the fake books, you have the transcribed solos, you have all of this information but you lose your identity. And it’s something that you have to really be careful of because when I was coming up we had to transcribe solos, you know we wrote them out and then we did the whole nine, but it was more for analysis versus well I want to sound like John, I want to sound like Hubert, I want to sound like whomever — Miles. We did it because that’s how musicians learned off the CDs during that time, or LPs. So you play along with the record, you learn it and then in the way you morph into your own thing versus you know verbatim. And you know Michael Brecker, he’s a friend of mine, he said the same thing. He was telling a lot of the young kids now man don’t play like me. Find somebody, find your own voice, find what you need to do but don’t — you have to find your thing that makes you feel good. And sometimes that’s a very difficult thing to tell young musicians that they have to find their own voice. You have to start working on that very early.
